title: One Year of COVID-19 Vaccine Misinformation on Twitter: Longitudinal Study
screen_reason: Twelve-month Twitter study of 294,081,599 English-language COVID-19-vaccine tweets. It reports (a) the share of vaccine tweets linking to low-credibility news domains (daily median 1.31%; ~1.5% of all tweets over the year), (b) the concentration of misinformation reshares in a small group of verified accounts (5.6% of posters earning 34.2% of low-credibility retweets), and (c) a within-misinformation validation share (approximately 76% of sampled low-credibility articles contained false or misleading content). All are quantitative shares with stated denominators.

estimates.country: not stated per country; English-language tweets that 'could originate from different countries'
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-vaccine tweets and retweets that share a link to a low-credibility news source (daily median over 2021)
estimates.value_raw: Daily percentage of vaccine tweets and retweets that share links to low-credibility news sources, median 1.31% (mainstream comparator median 7.53%); the whole-year aggregate is given in the text as 'only 1.5%' vs approximately 7.8% for mainstream sources
estimates.denominator: 294,081,599 English-language COVID-19-vaccine tweets (originals and retweets) shared by 19,581,249 unique users, collected with a list of almost 80 keywords via the Twitter filter API (median 720,575 tweets/day)
estimates.definition: The tweet contains a link whose top-level domain matches the merged low-credibility list (Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo, 674 sources, plus NewsGuard trust score <= 30, 1,181 sites; 1,718 domains in total)
estimates.misinfo_def: "the first approach identified tweets sharing links to low-credibility websites that were labeled by journalists, fact-checkers, and media experts for repeatedly sharing false news, hoaxes, conspiracy theories, unsubstantiated claims, hyperpartisan propaganda, click-bait, and so on"
estimates.source_quote: Figure 3. Comparisons between prevalence of tweets linking to mainstream and low-credibility sources. (A) Daily percentage of vaccine tweets and retweets that share links to low-credibility news sources (median: 1.31%) and mainstream news sources (median: 7.53%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Prevalence and Contagion of Online Misinformation', Figure 3 caption (p. 6); Figure 4C and 'Most Popular Misinformation Sources' (p. 6-7)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Merged domain list of 1,718 low-credibility sources: Iffy+ Misinfo/Disinfo (674 sources, built mainly on Media Bias/Fact Check 'Very Low'/'Low' factual reporting and 'Questionable'/'Conspiracy-Pseudoscience' labels, plus fake-news sites flagged by BuzzFeed, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact and Wikipedia) and NewsGuard trust score <= 30 (1,181 sites; the authors used a stricter cut than NewsGuard's own <60). Validated by two authors independently coding 50 random low-credibility links (38 misinformation, 7 factual, 4 unverified, 1 excluded), i.e. approximately 76% carried false or misleading content. Shortened URLs were resolved via HTTP requests.
estimates.moderator_quote: "Starting with covid and vaccine as our initial seeds, we employed a snowball sampling technique to identify co-occurring relevant keywords in December 2020 [52,53]. The resulting list contained almost 80 keywords... In this study, we analyzed the data collected in the period from January 4 to December 31, 2021. This comprises 294,081,599 tweets shared by 19,581,249 unique users"
estimates.notes: Time series collapsed to ONE representative point per the instructions: I use the DAILY MEDIAN 1.31% (printed exactly in the Figure 3A caption) rather than the whole-year aggregate, which the text gives only as 'only 1.5%' (approximate, read off Figure 4C). Both numbers are recorded in value_raw so an adjudicator can swap them; they differ because the low-credibility share rose significantly across the year (Mann-Kendall P<.001). Coded CONTENT, not SHARING, because the denominator is EVERY tweet in the keyword corpus (originals and retweets, with or without a link), i.e. all items that exist in the corpus - not the set of shared links. If the review's convention is instead to treat any Twitter corpus figure as SHARING content_share, this row should be recoded; the numerator is unchanged either way. breadth is empty because the numerator is defined by a source-level reliability list.

estimates.country: not stated per country; English-language tweets
estimates.measure_type: Twitter-verified accounts as a share of accounts posting low-credibility vaccine news, and their share of the retweets that content earned
estimates.value_raw: median daily proportion of verified accounts among posters of low-credibility news = 5.6%; median daily proportion of retweets earned by verified posters of low-credibility news = 34.2% (n = 828 verified accounts sharing low-credibility vaccine content over the year)
estimates.conc_group_label: Twitter-verified accounts among the accounts posting links to low-credibility vaccine news (n = 828 over the year; 'superspreaders')
estimates.denominator: All accounts posting links to low-credibility vaccine news in the corpus, and all retweets of that low-credibility content (daily proportions over 362 days)
estimates.definition: Account carries Twitter's 'verified' badge and posted a tweet linking to a domain on the merged low-credibility list; share measured as the proportion of retweets of low-credibility vaccine content earned by such accounts
estimates.misinfo_def: "we identified misinformation at the domain level based on a list of low-credibility sources (website domains) compiled by professional fact-checkers and journalists"
estimates.n: 828 verified accounts sharing low-credibility vaccine content (vs 98,612 verified accounts sharing vaccine content in general)
estimates.source_quote: The median daily proportions of verified accounts among posters of vaccine content, low-credibility news, and inaccessible YouTube videos are 15.4%, 5.6%, and 4.5%, respectively. The median daily proportions of retweets earned by verified posters of vaccine content, low-credibility news, and inaccessible YouTube videos are 43.1%, 34.2%, and 13.2%, respectively.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Superspreaders of Misinformation' (p. 7); Figure 5 caption (p. 8); Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same merged 1,718-domain low-credibility list; 'verified' is Twitter's own badge ('authentic, notable, and active'), not a researcher classification
estimates.moderator_quote: "Figure 5 shows that over time, verified accounts represented approximately 15% of those that posted vaccine content, but were consistently responsible for approximately 43% of that content."
estimates.notes: R1 satisfied: both halves are printed verbatim in the Figure 5 caption (5.6% of posters, 34.2% of retweets). Note the mild unit mismatch the paper itself carries: 5.6% and 34.2% are MEDIANS OF DAILY proportions, while n=828 is the year-long count of distinct verified accounts. The group is defined by Twitter verification, not by volume, so this is not a 'top X% by activity' concentration in the strict sense - it is a named subgroup whose activity share vastly exceeds its population share; population_scope 'other' because verified accounts are a mix of media outlets, public figures and organisations rather than the general public.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors independently visited each of 50 randomly selected low-credibility links and researched the claims; disagreements resolved by discussion to a single label; no kappa reported. The authors note that 6 of the 7 'factual' articles came from state propaganda outlets with a selection bias.
estimates.moderator_quote: "We tested the reliability of this domain-based approach to identify misinformation through a qualitative approach similar to that adopted in previous studies [38,60]. We randomly chose 50 low-credibility links in our data set and manually coded them as either 'factual,' 'misinformation,' or 'unverified.'"
estimates.notes: SOURCE_QUOTE IS TRUNCATED because the text file interleaves the PDF's two columns line by line, so no longer contiguous verbatim span exists. The full sentence reads: 'Our analysis based on a sample of articles suggests that approximately 76% of articles from low-credibility sources do contain false or misleading content.' (Discussion, limitations). R3 case: falsity computed INSIDE a misinformation-only sample (the denominator is links already flagged as low-credibility), so within_misinfo_content=true - keep for the appendix, never pool with population prevalence. The value is stated verbatim ('approximately 76%') and reproduced by 38/50; note 38/49 = 77.6% if the excluded blog post is removed from the denominator, and that the 4 'unverified' (dead) links sit in the denominator as non-misinformation, which biases the estimate downward.

estimates.n: vaccine tweets containing YouTube links (exact count not reported; daily median 0.52% of tweets)

estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Prevalence and Contagion of Online Misinformation' (p. 6); Figure 2D; Methods, 'Identifying Online Misinformation' (p. 5)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: No content judgement at all: the label is the video's accessibility status returned by the YouTube API, checked in March 2022 (at least 2 months after the last video was posted, against an estimated 41-day average removal lag). The authors cite prior work finding most inaccessible vaccine videos are antivaccine, and explicitly warn that videos can be inaccessible for restricted access or copyright and that these should be read as lower-bound estimates.
estimates.moderator_quote: "Similar limitations exist with respect to labeling inaccessible YouTube videos as 'low credibility.' For example, some of these videos may be inaccessible due to restricted access or copyright violations. An uploader's choice to restrict access to a video may serve as a way to circumvent content moderation policies or could be unrelated to antivaccination efforts... As such, analyses of inaccessible videos should be treated more as lower-bound estimates."
estimates.notes: SOURCE_QUOTE IS TRUNCATED because the text file interleaves the PDF's two columns line by line, so no longer contiguous verbatim span exists. The full sentence reads: 'Overall, the fraction of vaccine-related tweets linking to YouTube videos was very small (daily median: 0.52%). However, a nonnegligible proportion of these posts (daily median: 10.95%) shared links to inaccessible videos, with a larger prevalence in the first half of 2021 (a peak of 45% was observed in July) and a significant decreasing trend toward the end of the year (see Figure 2D).' JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator. Coded QUALITY + borderline=true, not CONTENT, under the governing rule that CONTENT requires items to be judged for truth/falsity against an external ground truth (fact-checks, expert verification, explicit false/misleading coding, or a source-reliability list). Video inaccessibility is a platform-moderation-status proxy: a wholly true video can receive the label (copyright takedown, uploader privacy change), which is exactly the test the instructions give for QUALITY, and the authors concede the point themselves. The paper nevertheless presents it as a misinformation-prevalence measure and cites validation that most such videos are antivaccine, so a reviewer who wants it as CONTENT (ground_truth 'classifier') has a defensible case; I flagged rather than dropped it. Time series collapsed to the reported daily median (10.95%), with the July peak of 45% recorded in value_raw.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Single-source and top-N concentration figures that R1 cannot accept because the paper never states the group as a % of sources/users: 'CHD accounted for approximately 18% of all tweets linking to low-credibility sources', 'the aggregated 20 most shared sources generated approximately 61% of all such tweets', and 'Retweets of Mr. Kennedy's tweets singularly accounted for 13.4% of all retweets of low-credibility vaccine content' (abstract: 'over 13%'). The number of distinct low-credibility domains or accounts actually observed in the corpus is not reported, so conc_group_pct cannot be derived without inventing a denominator (the 1,718-domain list includes domains never shared). These are strong concentration signals an adjudicator may want to capture under a looser rule. 2) 'CHD ... Accounting for approximately 0.30% of all vaccine tweets ... roughly twice the prevalence of CDC links (0.16%)' - a single-source share of the corpus; not extracted as a separate prevalence row because it is one outlet inside the 1.31% already recorded. 3) Verified accounts' share of ALL vaccine content (15.4% of posters, 43.1% of retweets) is a concentration of vaccine content generally, not of misinformation, so no row. 4) The parallel concentration figures for inaccessible YouTube videos (verified accounts 4.5% of posters, 13.2% of retweets, Figure 5) were not made into a row because the underlying measure is coded QUALITY/borderline here. 5) Figure 3B (median 89.19% of low-credibility tweets are retweets vs 67.96% for mainstream) describes the retweet composition of each class, not misinformation prevalence. 6) Bot scores (median daily average 0.22 / 0.25 / 0.26) are scale scores, not shares. 7) The mainstream comparators (7.53% daily median, ~7.8% aggregate) are recorded in value_raw of row 1 but are not misinformation estimates.

rob.design: Real-time Twitter filter-API collection (POST statuses/filter v1.1) on almost 80 English keywords snowballed from 'covid' and 'vaccine', 4 Jan - 31 Dec 2021: 294,081,599 tweets, 19,581,249 unique users, 8,160,838 unique URLs; keyword coverage validated (over 90% of tweets contain 'vaccine', 'vaccination' or 'vaccinate'). Misinformation identified at the DOMAIN level against a merged list of 1,718 low-credibility sources (Iffy+ 674 + NewsGuard score <= 30, 1,181), with a mainstream baseline of 2,765 NewsGuard >80 sources plus CDC and WHO; shortened URLs resolved. Domain labels validated by two authors independently coding 50 random low-credibility links (approximately 76% misinformation), with disagreements discussed to consensus; no kappa reported. A second, weaker measure labels YouTube videos 'suspicious' if inaccessible in March 2022. Bot activity from BotometerLite (validated against suspension status, Pearson r = 0.93). Robustness: results hold after removing @RobertKennedyJr; over 86% of low-credibility tweets come from the free Iffy+ list alone. Stated limitations: source-level labelling is imperfect in both directions, NewsGuard ratings are proprietary, inaccessible-video labels are lower bounds, BotometerLite is imperfect, and Twitter users are not representative of the general population; the aggregate analysis cannot separate countries.
